summary: Target-level completion of the accepted residual-image layer. It retains the 31 principal target IDs by reference, promotes the reusable carrier constructions and key comparisons, gives an all-field characteristic-two cocycle proof, supplies the primary semilinear automorphism proof, and exhibits an explicit tame niveau-two bad-dihedral Galois representation. The six existing planets are retained without adding duplicate landmarks. No formalisation is claimed.

nodes.title: Complex conjugation at a real place
nodes.statement: For a number field F, a real infinite place v, and an embedding ι:F̄→ℂ inducing v, construct the unique c_ι∈G_F satisfying ι(c_ι x)=conj(ι x) for every x∈F̄. Choose one such element c_v from v alone. It has order two. Any two choices over the same v are conjugate in G_F. The embedding is not an inverse map on all of ℂ: the inverse used in the construction is on the algebraic closure of ι(F) inside ℂ.
hypotheses: F is a number field; F̄ is AlgebraicClosure F; G_F has the Krull topology.
v is real; ι restricts to the unique real embedding of F inducing v.
proofSteps: Extend the real embedding F→ℝ→ℂ to F̄ using algebraic-closure embedding extension. Its image is precisely the elements of ℂ algebraic over that copy of F, so conjugation preserves the image.
Transport complex conjugation along this embedding. It fixes F and squares to the identity; a root of X²+1 in F̄ proves it is not the identity.
For another ι′ above v, the images coincide. The comparison g=ι⁻¹ι′ is an F-automorphism, and c_ι′=g⁻¹c_ιg. Choosing an extension gives c_v and its choice-independent conjugacy class.

sources.match: Serre fixes an embedding into ℂ and obtains the order-two Galois element used in oddness. The real-place and choice-comparison formulations here are the explicit number-field extension of that construction.

acceptance: Verify the intertwining identity on every element, not only roots of unity.
Two embeddings over one real place give the same determinant value for every representation.

nodes.title: Totally odd characters
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring A and a homomorphism μ:G_F→A×, IsTotallyOddChar μ means μ(c_v)=−1 for every real infinite place v of F. Continuity is required when μ is used as an arithmetic character, but is not part of this algebraic predicate. The condition is invariant under the choice of c_v. When F has no real places it is vacuous. The existing odd-representation node defines oddness of a rank-two finite projective representation by this predicate on its determinant character.
hypotheses: F is a number field and A a commutative ring.
A topological ring and a continuous character are used in arithmetic applications.
proofSteps: Use the complex-conjugation construction and impose the stated equalities at all real places.
A character kills conjugation because its target is commutative. Ring maps preserve −1. Restriction along G_L→G_F sends a real-place conjugation to one of F.
If A is reduced and 2=0, μ(c_v)²=1 implies (μ(c_v)−1)²=0 and hence μ(c_v)=1=−1. Without reducedness this implication fails.

sources.match: The determinant character takes value −1 at complex conjugation. Here the predicate is separated from the representation and imposed at all real places.

sources.locator: §1, first definition of S-type, preprint p. 2

nodes.title: Split Cartan subgroups
nodes.statement: For a two-dimensional k-vector space V and distinct one-dimensional subspaces D₁,D₂, split(D₁,D₂) is the subgroup of GL(V) preserving each line individually. It is naturally the product of the automorphism groups of the two lines, and after choosing a nonzero vector in each line it is (k×)². The definition uses ordered lines, but the subgroup is unchanged by swapping them. Its matrix model under an adapted basis is the already implemented TauCeti.diagonalTorus k 2.
hypotheses: k is a field; V has dimension two.
D₁ and D₂ are distinct lines; no cardinality bound is needed for the definition or comparison.
proofSteps: Distinct lines are complementary. Restriction of an automorphism to each summand gives the product equivalence; conversely combine two line automorphisms.

Transport along an adapted basis using Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup.toLin′. Diagonal matrices are exactly the operators preserving both coordinate lines, by the existing diagonal-torus membership theorem.
Conjugation carries each line to its image. For a finite k the order is (q−1)². When q=2 the subgroup is trivial, so its normaliser is all GL₂(F₂).

sources.match: Defines the subgroup preserving the two lines and identifies it with a product of multiplicative groups. The coordinate API here uses the existing Tau Ceti model.

acceptance: No new node for the coordinate diagonal torus or its normaliser quotient: those are baseline declarations.

nodes.title: Split half-Cartan subgroups
nodes.statement: For distinct lines D₁,D₂ in a plane V over k, halfSplit(D₁,D₂) consists of the automorphisms preserving D₁ and fixing D₂ pointwise. In an adapted basis it is diag(a,1), a∈k×. It is isomorphic to k× through the determinant. Multiplying it by the scalar subgroup gives split(D₁,D₂); both have the same projective image. For finite q≥3 it determines the unique split Cartan containing it.
hypotheses: k is a field and dim V=2; D₁,D₂ are distinct lines.
The uniqueness statement requires |k|≥3. Serre fixes the other ordered line; interchanging D₁,D₂ reconciles the conventions.
proofSteps: Use the direct-sum decomposition of V; an automorphism on D₁ together with the identity on D₂ is the required element.
In coordinates, determinant is a and every diagonal matrix diag(a,b) factors as the scalar b times diag(a/b,1).
For q≥3 choose a≠1. The two distinct eigenspaces of diag(a,1) force the two lines of any split Cartan containing the half-Cartan. The argument fails over F₂, where the half-Cartan is trivial.

sources.match: The subgroup fixing one line pointwise generates the split Cartan with scalars and supplies the half-Cartan hypotheses in image recognition.

acceptance: Use pointwise fixation of D₂; preserving D₂ merely gives the full split Cartan.

nodes.title: Basis-free non-split Cartan subgroups
nodes.statement: Let k be a finite field and V a k-vector space of dimension two. For a subalgebra E⊂End_k(V) that is a field and has dimension two over k, nonsplit(E) is the image of E× in GL(V). This is a basis-free unit subgroup, not a replacement for the existing coordinate TauCeti.GL2NonSplitTorus. V is free of rank one over E. An E-linear identification V≃E, followed by TauCeti.nonSplitTorusBasis, transports nonsplit(E) to that existing left-multiplication matrix subgroup.
hypotheses: k is finite; dim_k V=2.
E is an actual field subalgebra of End_k(V), not merely a two-dimensional commutative algebra.
proofSteps: The subalgebra inclusion is injective and maps units to invertible operators. Define the subgroup by the range of the induced unit homomorphism.
A nonzero v∈V makes a↦a v an injective k-linear map E→V because every nonzero a is invertible. Equal dimensions make it an equivalence and give the rank-one E-module description.
In these coordinates the action is left multiplication, exactly GL2NonSplitTorusHom. The existing norm, trace and cardinality formulas transfer along this equivalence.

sources.match: Defines the non-split Cartan by a quadratic field inside the endomorphism algebra. The coordinate identification is the transport to the existing library construction.

acceptance: For the regular representation V=E, compare the transported subgroup directly with GL2NonSplitTorus k E hE, not with a fresh unverified matrix model.

nodes.title: Semilinear description of Cartan normalisers
nodes.statement: For nonsplit(E), the normaliser consists of E-linear operators and operators semilinear for the nontrivial k-automorphism of E. Its quotient by nonsplit(E) is Aut_k(E), cyclic of order two. In E-coordinates, an element is x↦a x or x↦a x^q. The latter has trace zero and scalar square N_E/k(a). The projective Cartan has order q+1 and the projective normaliser is dihedral of order 2(q+1). For the split Cartan with q≥3, transport the already proved diagonal-normaliser quotient to get the permutation group on its two lines, and the analogous trace-zero, scalar-square and dihedral formulas with q−1.
hypotheses: k is finite; q=|k|; dim V=2.
The split case requires q≥3. The non-split case includes q=2.
proofSteps: Units of E span E as a k-algebra, so conjugation by a normaliser induces a k-algebra automorphism of E. Its kernel is the centraliser of E, which is E× because V is a one-dimensional E-module.
Every automorphism of E lifts on V≃E. The two automorphisms are identity and q-Frobenius. Compose Frobenius with multiplication by a to compute the square and trace (including characteristic two).

Modulo k× the action of Frobenius sends a to a^q≡a⁻¹. This proves the dihedral description. In the split case cite diagonalNormalizerQuotientMulEquivPerm and compute the off-diagonal matrices in an adapted basis.

sources.match: Gives the order-two normaliser quotient and the field-automorphism action. The trace, square and projective formulas are direct computations in that description.

acceptance: At q=2 only the non-split quotient has order two; the split quotient has order six.
At q=3 the split projective normaliser is the Klein four-group.

nodes.title: The unique Cartan of a regular semisimple element
nodes.statement: Let k be finite of characteristic different from two, V a plane and s∈GL(V). If Δ(s)=Tr(s)²−4det(s) is nonzero, then exactly one Cartan subgroup contains s. This Cartan is split iff Δ(s) is a square in k. In the split case its lines are the two eigenspaces; otherwise it is the unit group of the quadratic field k[s] inside End_k(V).
hypotheses: dim V=2; k finite; char k≠2; Δ(s)≠0.
proofSteps: The characteristic polynomial has distinct roots. If Δ is a square, its two k-rational eigenspaces give the split Cartan and force uniqueness.

Otherwise the characteristic polynomial is irreducible, k[s] is a quadratic field and s is in its unit subgroup. The existing centraliser theorem in a quadratic-extension basis shows that every commuting operator lies in this field.
Every Cartan containing s is commutative, hence is contained in this centraliser; equal orders give equality.

sources.match: The nonzero discriminant identifies the unique Cartan and determines whether it is split.

acceptance: diag(1,2) over F₅ has split Cartan; [[0,2],[1,0]] has the non-split F₂₅ Cartan.
The scalar identity has zero discriminant and lies in several Cartans, so the nonzero hypothesis cannot be omitted.

nodes.title: Cartans contained in a Cartan normaliser
nodes.statement: Let C be a Cartan subgroup of GL₂(F_p). A split Cartan C′ contained in N(C) equals C if p≥5; a split half-Cartan C′ contained in N(C) lies in C under the same bound. A non-split Cartan C′ contained in N(C) equals C if p≥3. These are the hypotheses of Serre Proposition 14, including the different bounds. Over F₃ the split-Cartan equality is false.
hypotheses: p is prime; p≥5 for the split and half-split alternatives; p≥3 for the non-split alternative.
proofSteps: Pass to the projective quotient. Its Cartan rotation subgroup is cyclic and its normaliser is dihedral; outside the rotations every element has order two.
The projective orders p−1 for split/half-split and p+1 for non-split are greater than two under the stated bounds. A generator must therefore lie in the rotation subgroup.

Lift through scalars and compare orders for full Cartans. For a half-Cartan multiply by scalars to recover the full split Cartan, using halfSplit_sup_center. At p=3 the rotation order is two, so the argument does not apply.

sources.locator: Proposition 14, printed p. 279; following remark, p. 280
sources.match: Proves the inclusions and records the split-Cartan exception at p=3.

acceptance: Keep the p=3 pair of distinct split Cartans with equal normaliser as a negative regression fixture.

nodes.title: The projective trace field
nodes.statement: For a subgroup G≤GL₂(k) over a field k, projectiveTraceField(G) is the smallest subfield of k containing Tr(g)²/det(g) for every g∈G. This scalar is unchanged by conjugation or multiplication of g by a scalar unit, so the field is an invariant of the projective image with its embedding in PGL₂(k). It is not defined as the field generated by the matrix entries. In the standard nonsolvable PSL₂/PGL₂ alternatives it is the coefficient field F₀ used by the accepted classification nodes.
hypotheses: k is a field; G is an actual subgroup of GL₂(k).
The descent and standard-image comparisons use the hypotheses of the accepted coefficient-field target; arbitrary projective groups are not asserted to descend to this field.
proofSteps: Take Subfield.closure of the stated set of scalars. The determinant is nonzero because g is invertible.
Trace is invariant under conjugation. Multiplication by λ scales trace by λ and determinant by λ², proving scalar invariance.

A field embedding carries the generators to the same expressions in the image group. For a standard subfield subgroup, evaluate diagonal and unipotent products as in the accepted Dickson coefficient-field proof; do not infer a coefficient field from entry values of a chosen conjugate.

sources.match: The projective classification and lifting to scalar multiples of a subfield group motivate making the coefficient field explicit. The closure by projective traces is the accepted parent convention and its nonsolvable comparison is retained there.
The root-group argument recovers the field of a standard PSL₂/PGL₂ subgroup; the trace-field API records the invariant field rather than an arbitrary matrix realization.

acceptance: A group conjugate over a larger field to a standard subfield subgroup retains its projective trace field.

Pins the coefficient field of the commutator SL₂ group and the containing scalar-GL₂ group.

nodes.title: The cyclotomic square subfield
nodes.statement: For a number field F and an odd prime p, let K=F(ζ_p) inside F̄ and H=Gal(K/F). Define cyclotomicSquareSubfield(F,p) as the lift to F̄ of the fixed field K^{H²}, where H²={h²:h∈H}; H is cyclic, so these squares form a subgroup. This field E equals F if [K:F] is odd, and is the unique quadratic subextension of K/F if the degree is even. For F=ℚ it is ℚ(√p*) with p*=(−1)^((p−1)/2)p, also the field generated by a primitive quadratic Gauss sum. Formation of E is not asserted to commute with arbitrary base change.
hypotheses: F is a number field; p is an odd prime.
K is the actual cyclotomic extension, whose Galois group can be a proper subgroup of F_p×.
proofSteps: Use the action on a primitive p-th root of unity to inject H into F_p×. The resulting cyclic group has a square subgroup of index one or two according to its parity.
Apply fixedField and lift for the concrete intermediate field in K. Finite Galois correspondence gives the degree and unique quadratic-subfield assertions.

Over ℚ, galEquivZMod identifies H with all F_p×. The quadratic Gauss sum transforms by the quadratic character and its square is p*. The baseline gaussSum_sq supplies the square identity; this nonrational Gauss sum generates the index-two fixed field.

sources.locator: §1.5, Definition 1.12 and proof of Lemma 1.13, preprint pp. 7–8
sources.match: Uses the quadratic subfield of ℚ(ζ_p) for the residual restriction criterion. The number-field square-subgroup construction here is an explicit generalization; it does not replace it by F(√p*) uniformly.

acceptance: For F=ℚ(√5), p=5, E=F(ζ₅) while F(√p*)=F. This prevents the incorrect uniform square-root definition.

api.name: TauCeti.GaloisRep.cyclotomicSubfield
api.statement: Adjoin the primitive p-th roots to F inside F̄.

api.name: TauCeti.GaloisRep.cyclotomicSquareSubfield

api.name: TauCeti.GaloisRep.cyclotomicSquareSubfield_le

api.name: TauCeti.GaloisRep.cyclotomicSquareSubfield_degree

nodes.title: Automorphisms of the projective linear groups
nodes.statement: For a finite field k with q≥4, every automorphism of PSL₂(k) is the composite of conjugation by an element of PGL₂(k) and entrywise application of a field automorphism of k. These factors are unique in PGL₂(k) and Aut(k). Thus Aut(PSL₂(k))≃PΓL₂(k). Restriction from Aut(PGL₂(k)) to Aut(PSL₂(k)) is an isomorphism, so Aut(PGL₂(k)) has the same semilinear description. There is no additional graph automorphism in type A₁.
hypotheses: k is a finite field with q≥4; the automorphisms are automorphisms of finite abstract groups.
Inner-diagonal means conjugation by PGL₂(k), not only by PSL₂(k).
proofSteps: Specialize Steinberg Theorem 3.2 to type A₁. His §5.1 normalizes a pair of opposite Sylow subgroups by an inner automorphism; §5.2 normalizes a chosen root generator by a diagonal automorphism.

Write the induced map on upper root elements as x₊(a)↦x₊(f(a)). Addition follows from the root-group law. The rank-one relations of §4.10 and §5.7 recover field multiplication: in characteristic two use surjectivity of squaring, and in odd characteristic polarize the square relation. The lower root subgroup is determined by the Weyl element.

The two root subgroups generate, so the normalized automorphism is the entrywise field automorphism. A semilinear operator centralizing PSL₂(k) has trivial field component and scalar linear component, proving uniqueness.

The derived subgroup of PGL₂(k) is its characteristic PSL₂(k). An automorphism restricting to the identity changes every element by something centralizing PSL₂(k); this centralizer in PGL₂(k) is trivial. Every semilinear automorphism extends, giving the restriction isomorphism.

sources.locator: Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3, printed p. 608; §§4.10, 5.1–5.2, 5.7 and completion of proof, pp. 610–613
sources.match: The theorem decomposes automorphisms into graph, field, diagonal and inner components. For A₁ the graph component is trivial; the cited proof reconstructs the field map from root-group parameters. The PGL₂ extension is the derived-subgroup argument given here.

acceptance: At q=4 the result identifies Aut(A₅) with S₅, including the nontrivial field automorphism.
At q=9 both the diagonal outer automorphism and the field automorphism of A₆ are present.

nodes.title: Matrix cocycles for SL₂ in characteristic two
nodes.statement: Let k₀ be a finite field of characteristic two with q≥4, let k be any extension field, and let SL₂(k₀) act on M₂(k) by conjugation through entrywise inclusion. Every function f:SL₂(k₀)→M₂(k) satisfying f(gh)=f(g)+g f(h)g⁻¹ is of the form f(g)=g Xg⁻¹−X for one X∈M₂(k). Equivalently H¹(SL₂(k₀),M₂(k))=0. This is an all-q proof, not an extrapolation from computations at q=4,8,16.
hypotheses: q=2^r with r≥2; k₀→k is a field embedding; no finiteness of k is required.
Coefficients are all matrices, not the trace-zero submodule or the quotient by scalars.
proofSteps: Average f over T={diag(a,a⁻¹):a∈k₀×}; |T|=q−1 is odd and invertible in k. Subtract its coboundary to arrange f|_T=0.

Put u(t)=[[1,t],[0,1]] and f(u(t))=[[A(t),B(t)],[C(t),D(t)]]. The identity u(t)²=1 and the cocycle identity imply C(t)=0 and A(t)=D(t) for t≠0; f(1)=0 covers t=0. The root-group law then makes A and B additive.

Conjugation by diag(a,a⁻¹) gives A(a²t)=A(t) and B(a²t)=a²B(t). Squaring is bijective on k₀, so A is constant on nonzero t. Since q≥4 choose distinct nonzero t,s with t+s≠0; additivity forces that constant to be zero. The second identity gives B(t)=t B(1).
Subtract the coboundary of diag(B(1),0), which is T-fixed and takes u(t) to t B(1)E₁₂. The cocycle now vanishes on the upper Borel B=TU.

The cocycle is constant on right B-cosets. Average its values over G/B, of cardinal q+1, again odd and invertible. Left multiplication permutes these cosets, and the cocycle equation shows that the average supplies a global coboundary. This proves the asserted vanishing for every r≥2 and every extension field.

sources.match: States the vanishing and attributes it to Dickinson Lemma 42. Dickinson is not claimed read. The explicit torus/root-group/odd-index averaging proof in this node replaces the previously missing proof.
Independently records self-extension vanishing when r>1; it is corroboration only. Its cited Ext calculation is not used as an unread input to the elementary proof here.

acceptance: In the root calculation use all matrices: removing scalar matrices changes the cohomology problem.
The argument needs q≥4 to kill the constant diagonal function on nonzero root parameters.

nodes.title: An explicit niveau-two bad-dihedral representation
nodes.statement: Let L be the splitting field over ℚ of X⁴+3, with α⁴=−3 and i²=−1, so L=ℚ(α,i). Its Galois group is D₈, with r(α)=iα, r(i)=i, s(α)=α, s(i)=−i. Define the representation over F₃ by r↦R=[[0,−1],[1,0]], s↦S=diag(1,−1), and compose with G_ℚ→Gal(L/ℚ). It is continuous, faithful on Gal(L/ℚ), odd and absolutely irreducible. The subgroup fixing ℚ(√−3)=ℚ(ζ₃) is ⟨r²,s⟩ and acts diagonally, so the representation is bad dihedral. At 3, tame inertia is ⟨r⟩ of order four; over F₉ its characters are ω₂² and ω₂⁶. Thus b=2 satisfies (3+1)/2 dividing b and the projective inertia image has order two.
hypotheses: p=3; the coefficient field is F₃ and absolute irreducibility is tested after coefficient extension.
Choose α with complex argument π/4; then complex conjugation is r³s. The inertial eigencharacters are unordered.
proofSteps: X⁴+3 is Eisenstein at 3. Over K=ℚ(α²)=ℚ(√−3), adjoining i is unramified quadratic at 3 (−1 is a nonsquare unit in the residue F₃), whereas adjoining α is ramified quadratic because α² is a uniformizer of K₃. The quadratic extensions are distinct. Thus [L:ℚ]=8; r and s give the displayed D₈ presentation.

The matrices satisfy R⁴=S²=1 and SRS=R⁻¹. Their F₃-span as group elements is all M₂(F₃), so the representation is absolutely irreducible; the resulting D₈ matrix map is injective. Complex conjugation r³s has determinant −1.
r² and s fix α² and act by −I and diag(1,−1), so restriction to K splits. This is the bad-dihedral definition at p=3.

Locally at 3, ℚ₃(i)/ℚ₃ is unramified quadratic and X⁴+3 is Eisenstein over it. The ramification index is four and the full extension has degree eight, so inertia is precisely ⟨r⟩; its order is prime to 3.

A primitive level-two character has order eight. R has eigenvalues i and −i in F₉, which have exponents 2 and 6 relative to a primitive eighth root (changing the fundamental-character choice permutes these two). Their ratio is −1, giving projective order two.

sources.locator: §1.5, proof of Lemma 1.14 and Remark 5, preprint p. 9
sources.match: Supplies the projective-inertia and niveau-two divisibility criterion tested by this example. The polynomial and the explicit D₈ construction are a calculation of this packet, not an example attributed to the source.

acceptance: Compute all eight matrices and their span, determinant and restriction subgroup.
Verify the local ramification calculation, not just an abstract representation of D₈.
